imageCaption: A jaguar resting beside a flooded Amazon forest channel.
diet: Carnivore — caiman, capybara, peccary, fish and turtles
distribution: From Mexico through Central America to northern Argentina; strongest populations remain in the Amazon and Pantanal.
habitat: Tropical rainforest, seasonally flooded forest, river margins, wetlands and dry woodland.
physical: A stocky big cat with a broad head, powerful jaws and a coat of rosettes. Individuals can be identified by their unique spot patterns.
behaviour: Solitary and territorial. Unlike most big cats, jaguars are powerful swimmers and often hunt along rivers and flooded forest.
reproduction: Gestation lasts about 90–105 days. Females give birth to one to four cubs, usually in a sheltered den; cubs stay with their mother for around two years.
description: The largest cat of the Americas and the third-largest cat in the world. Its extraordinary bite can pierce turtle shells and caiman skulls, and its presence shapes prey behaviour across the forest.
keyTraits: Strongest bite force relative to body size among big cats
Rosette patterns are unique to each individual
An important apex predator in Amazonian river and forest systems

imageCaption: A Harpy Eagle in captivity; wild birds are elusive canopy specialists.
diet: Carnivore — sloths, monkeys, opossums and large birds
distribution: Lowland tropical forests from southern Mexico through Central America to northern Argentina.
habitat: Mature lowland and premontane rainforest with tall emergent trees for nesting.
physical: A massive raptor with a double crest, a pale grey head, dark chest band and enormous talons. Females are larger than males.
behaviour: Hunts by stealth from perches below the canopy, using short bursts of flight to seize prey. Pairs maintain large territories and reuse nest trees.
reproduction: Pairs typically raise one chick every two to three years. Nests are huge platforms of sticks built high in emergent trees.
description: One of the world's largest and most powerful eagles. Its rear talons are longer than a grizzly bear's claws, allowing it to take prey as large as howler monkeys.
keyTraits: Apex aerial predator of the Neotropical canopy
Facial disc helps funnel sound to the ears
Needs large areas of undisturbed forest to breed successfully

imageCaption: An endemic Yakushima macaque on a moss-covered branch.
diet: Omnivore — fruit, seeds, fungi, leaves, insects and small animals
distribution: Restricted to Yakushima Island, Japan.
habitat: Subtropical and temperate rainforest from coastal forest to mountain cedar stands.
physical: A dark-furred macaque with a short tail and dense coat adapted to heavy rain and cool mountain temperatures.
behaviour: Lives in structured social troops. Famous for occasionally riding or closely associating with Sika deer, apparently benefiting from fruit dropped by the deer.
reproduction: Females usually produce one infant after a gestation of about five to six months. Infants remain dependent for several years.
description: An endemic island subspecies of the Japanese macaque, adapted to Yakushima's extraordinary rainfall. Its forest life is interwoven with the island's mossy cedar ecosystem.
keyTraits: Dense coat adapted to persistent rain
Known for unusual associations with Sika deer

imageCaption: A Sika deer grazing on a mossy Yakushima forest floor.
diet: Herbivore — grasses, leaves, herbs and forest fruit
distribution: Yakushima Island, Japan.
habitat: Mossy subtropical forest, forest edges and open areas across the island.
physical: A relatively small, dark-coated sika deer with spotted summer coat and compact antlers in males.
behaviour: Browses and grazes in small groups. High population density can suppress forest understorey regeneration.
reproduction: Mating peaks in autumn; one calf is typically born after about seven months.
description: Yakushima's endemic sika deer is a key herbivore in the island forest. Its relationship with the endemic macaque is one of the more unusual ecological associations in East Asian forests.
keyTraits: A major force shaping understorey vegetation

statusLabel: Least Concern (locally endangered in parts of western Europe)
imageCaption: A Carpathian lynx portrait.
diet: Carnivore — roe deer, chamois, hares and smaller mammals
distribution: Boreal and temperate forests from Scandinavia and eastern Europe across Russia and Central Asia, with reintroduced populations in western Europe.
habitat: Dense mixed and coniferous forest with good cover, rocky terrain and sufficient prey.
physical: A medium-sized wild cat with long legs, tufted ears, a short bobbed tail and large snowshoe-like paws.
behaviour: Solitary and secretive, holding large territories. Uses scent marking, scrapes and vocalisations to communicate.
reproduction: Mating occurs in late winter. After a gestation of about 69 days, females give birth to two to four kittens in a hidden den.
description: The largest European wild cat. Persecuted to local extinction in parts of Europe, it is now returning through reintroduction and natural recolonisation, including in Germany's Black Forest.
keyTraits: A flagship species for forest connectivity and rewilding
references: Black Forest National Park — lynx monitoring

imageCaption: A European bison calf in Białowieża Forest.
diet: Herbivore — grasses, bark, leaves and acorns
distribution: Free-ranging herds in Poland, Belarus, Germany, Romania and several other European countries, descended from captive breeding stock.
habitat: Mixed deciduous and coniferous forest with open clearings, meadows and wetlands.
physical: Europe's heaviest wild land mammal, with a massive forequarter, a high shoulder hump and short, curved horns.
behaviour: Lives in herds led by older females; males may be solitary or form small bachelor groups. Bison browse and break vegetation, creating structural diversity.
reproduction: Females give birth to a single calf after about nine months, usually in spring. Herds protect calves collectively.
description: The European bison survived the 20th century only through intense breeding and reintroduction. Białowieża remains its most important stronghold and a symbol of European rewilding.
keyTraits: Europe's heaviest surviving wild land mammal
A living remnant of Pleistocene megafauna
An ecosystem engineer that maintains open woodland structure
references: Białowieża National Park — European bison programme

imageCaption: An African forest elephant in dense Congo Basin vegetation.
diet: Herbivore — fruit, leaves, bark, roots and mineral-rich soil
distribution: West and Central African tropical forests, especially the Congo Basin.
habitat: Lowland tropical rainforest, swamp forest and forest-savanna mosaics.
physical: Smaller than the savanna elephant, with rounded ears, a straighter back and downward-pointing tusks adapted to dense forest.
behaviour: Moves along traditional forest trails and clearings, dispersing seeds in large quantities. Social groups are smaller and less fluid than those of savanna elephants.
reproduction: Females give birth to one calf after a gestation of around 22 months, one of the longest pregnancies among mammals.
description: A critically endangered forest specialist and one of the most important seed dispersers in the Congo Basin. Its decline threatens the composition and regeneration of vast areas of rainforest.
keyTraits: Disperses seeds of many large-fruited trees
Creates trails and clearings used by other species

imageCaption: An okapi, whose striped legs help it disappear into forest shadow.
diet: Folivore — leaves, buds, shoots and fruit
distribution: Endemic to the northeastern Democratic Republic of Congo, including the Ituri Forest.
habitat: Dense lowland rainforest understorey and gallery forest.
physical: A giraffe relative with a long neck, large ears, a dark velvety coat and striking black-and-white stripes on the legs and hindquarters.
behaviour: Solitary and extremely secretive. Uses large ears and a long prehensile tongue to browse vegetation; males defend territories.
reproduction: Females give birth to a single calf after a gestation of about 14–16 months. Calves may remain hidden for weeks.
description: The okapi is the only living relative of the giraffe. It was unknown to Western science until 1901 and remains one of the rainforest's most elusive large mammals.
keyTraits: Endemic to the eastern DR Congo
Only living relative of the giraffe
Striped legs provide camouflage in dappled forest light

imageCaption: A western lowland gorilla close-up.
diet: Herbivore — leaves, stems, shoots, fruit, bark and insects
distribution: Lowland tropical forests of the Congo Basin, including Gabon, Congo, Cameroon and the Central African Republic.
habitat: Dense lowland rainforest, swamp forest and forest clearings.
physical: A stocky great ape with dark hair, a pronounced brow ridge and strong sexual dimorphism; mature males develop silver backs.
behaviour: Lives in social groups led by a dominant silverback. Uses a complex repertoire of vocalisations, gestures and facial expressions.
reproduction: Females give birth to one infant after about 8.5–9 months. Interbirth intervals can exceed four years.
description: The most widespread gorilla subspecies, yet critically endangered because of poaching, disease and habitat loss. Its survival depends on large, well-protected forest blocks.
keyTraits: Key seed disperser in Congo Basin forests

imageCaption: A female Bengal tiger.
diet: Carnivore — spotted deer, wild boar, monkeys and other vertebrates
distribution: The Sundarbans population lives in the mangrove delta shared by Bangladesh and India; the wider Bengal tiger range includes India, Nepal, Bhutan and Bangladesh.
habitat: Mangrove forest, tidal creeks, freshwater swamp and tropical moist forest.
physical: A large orange-and-black striped cat with a powerful build. Sundarbans tigers are adapted to swimming and moving through soft tidal mud.
behaviour: Solitary and territorial. Sundarbans tigers regularly swim between islands and are known to drink brackish water.
reproduction: Females give birth to two to four cubs after a gestation of about 100–110 days, usually in dense cover.
description: The tiger is the largest living cat. The Sundarbans population is especially significant because it lives entirely within mangrove forest and is exposed to cyclones, sea-level rise and human-wildlife conflict.
keyTraits: Strong swimmer adapted to tidal mangrove habitat
Apex predator of the Sundarbans ecosystem

imageCaption: A fishing cat, a wetland specialist of South and Southeast Asia.
diet: Carnivore — fish, crabs, molluscs, frogs and small mammals
distribution: Fragmented populations in South and Southeast Asia, including the Sundarbans, Sri Lanka and parts of Thailand and Java.
habitat: Mangroves, marshes, reed beds, rivers and wetlands.
physical: A stocky, semi-aquatic cat with a broad head, short legs, partially webbed toes and a coarse olive-grey coat with dark spots.
behaviour: An excellent swimmer that hunts in shallow water, often using its paws to stir up prey. Solitary and secretive.
reproduction: Gestation lasts about 63–70 days. Females raise two to three kittens in a sheltered den.
description: A specialized wetland predator that is rarely seen and easily overlooked. Draining and conversion of wetlands are its greatest threats.

imageCaption: The iridescent Resplendent Quetzal in Monteverde cloud forest.
diet: Frugivore — wild avocado, laurel and other cloud-forest fruit; occasionally insects
size: 35–40 cm body length; males with tail streamers up to 1 m
distribution: Highland cloud forests from southern Mexico through Central America to western Panama.
habitat: Undisturbed tropical montane cloud forest with mature fruiting trees for nesting and feeding.
physical: Males have iridescent green plumage, a red breast, a yellow bill and long green tail streamers. The colour is structural rather than pigment-based.
behaviour: Feeds mainly on fruit, often swallowing whole avocados and later regurgitating seeds. Males perform aerial displays and compete for nest cavities.
reproduction: Pairs excavate or reuse a cavity in a decaying tree. Two eggs are incubated for about 18 days; both parents care for the chicks.
description: A sacred bird of Mesoamerican cultures and one of the most spectacular cloud-forest species. It is highly sensitive to forest disturbance and depends on mature fruiting trees.
keyTraits: Males have iridescent tail streamers up to one metre long
An important seed disperser for wild avocado trees

statusLabel: Least Concern (Australian population is of conservation concern)
imageCaption: Daintree rainforest habitat of the Southern Cassowary.
diet: Frugivore — fallen rainforest fruit, fungi and small animals
distribution: New Guinea, surrounding islands and the Wet Tropics of north-eastern Queensland, Australia.
habitat: Tropical rainforest, gallery forest, swamp forest and forest edges.
physical: A large flightless bird with glossy black feathers, a bright blue neck, a casque on the head and powerful legs with dagger-like claws.
behaviour: Solitary outside breeding. An important seed disperser that swallows large fruits and moves seeds long distances through the forest.
reproduction: Females lay three to five eggs in a ground nest. Males incubate the eggs and raise the chicks alone for many months.
description: A keystone rainforest species and one of the world's largest birds. Road collisions, dog attacks and habitat fragmentation are major threats in Australia.
keyTraits: Males alone incubate eggs and raise chicks
Dangerous when cornered, with powerful clawed feet
references: Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service — cassowary conservation

imageCaption: Small riparian birds foraging along the Cheonggyecheon.
diet: Granivore and insectivore — seeds, grain and small invertebrates
activity: Diurnal, most active at dawn and dusk
distribution: Widespread across Europe and Asia; introduced in parts of North America and Australia.
habitat: Woodland edges, farmland, villages, parks and urban riparian corridors.
physical: A small brown sparrow with a chestnut crown, black ear patch and white cheek.
behaviour: Highly social, often feeding in flocks. Uses cavities and crevices for nesting, including buildings and river walls.
reproduction: Typically raises two or three broods per year, with four to six eggs per clutch.
description: A resilient songbird that has adapted well to people. Along the Cheonggyecheon it forages among river stones and bathes in the shallow water.

imageCaption: Wading birds along the restored Cheonggyecheon river corridor.
diet: Carnivore — fish, amphibians, crustaceans and small mammals
distribution: Widespread across Europe, Asia and Africa.
habitat: Rivers, lakes, marshes, estuaries, rice fields and urban waterways.
physical: A tall grey wading bird with a long neck, dagger-like yellow bill and long legs.
behaviour: An ambush hunter that stands motionless in shallow water before striking with a rapid neck movement. Usually solitary when foraging, often colonial when nesting.
reproduction: Nests in trees or reed beds, often in colonies. Three to five eggs are incubated for about four weeks.
description: A familiar indicator of healthy wetlands and rivers. Its return to the Cheonggyecheon became a visible symbol of the stream's ecological recovery.
keyTraits: Apex wading predator of shallow water

imageCaption: Scarlet macaws in flight over the Amazon canopy.
diet: Frugivore and granivore — fruit, seeds and nuts
distribution: Lowland tropical forests from southern Mexico through Central America to the Amazon Basin.
habitat: Mature tropical rainforest, riverine forest and forest edges.
physical: A brilliant scarlet parrot with blue and yellow wing feathers, a white facial patch and a hooked bill.
behaviour: Pairs bond for life and fly together, often calling loudly. Intelligent, social and dependent on large trees for nesting.
reproduction: Nests in tree cavities. Two to four eggs are incubated for around five weeks.
description: One of the most recognisable Neotropical birds. Its large range helps it persist, but local declines follow hunting, trapping and loss of old nesting trees.

imageCaption: Boyd's forest dragon in the Daintree rainforest.
diet: Insectivore — insects, worms and other small invertebrates
distribution: Restricted to the Wet Tropics rainforests of north-eastern Queensland, Australia.
habitat: Lowland and upland tropical rainforest, especially along forest tracks and tree trunks.
physical: A small agamid lizard with a distinctive angular head, spiny crest, cryptic colouration and a long tail.
behaviour: Expert at camouflage, often remaining motionless on tree trunks. It relies on the dappled light of the rainforest to avoid detection.
reproduction: Females lay small clutches of eggs in moist soil or leaf litter.
description: A rainforest endemic that is rarely far from a tree trunk. Its restricted range makes it a flagship for Wet Tropics conservation.
references: Atlas of Living Australia — Lophosaurus boydii

imageCaption: The golden toad of Monteverde, preserved in a historical photograph.
diet: Insectivore — small arthropods
distribution: Known only from a small area of cloud forest near Monteverde, Costa Rica.
habitat: High-elevation cloud forest, breeding in temporary pools among mossy roots.
physical: Males were brilliant golden-orange; females were darker with red spots. The species was highly sexually dimorphic.
behaviour: Males gathered in large numbers around temporary pools during the early rainy season to compete for mates.
reproduction: Breeding was explosive and tied to rain. Eggs were laid in shallow pools; larvae developed rapidly.
description: The golden toad vanished abruptly in 1989 and was declared extinct. Its disappearance became a global symbol of amphibian declines linked to climate change, disease and habitat vulnerability.
keyTraits: Endemic to a tiny cloud-forest area
A symbol of global amphibian decline

imageCaption: Clear, oxygenated shallows of the Cheonggyecheon — sweetfish habitat.
diet: Herbivore — algae and biofilm on river stones
distribution: Rivers and coastal waters of East Asia, including Japan, Korea, China and Taiwan.
habitat: Clear, fast-flowing rivers with gravel and cobble beds; migrates between freshwater and coastal waters.
physical: A slender, silvery fish with a small mouth and a distinctive sweet, melon-like scent when fresh.
behaviour: Grazes algae from rocks and defends feeding territories. Sensitive to poor water quality and barriers to migration.
reproduction: Adults spawn in autumn; larvae drift downstream to the sea and juveniles migrate back upstream in spring.
description: Prized as a food fish and a sensitive indicator of clean, connected rivers. Its return to the restored Cheonggyecheon was celebrated as a conservation milestone.
keyTraits: Migratory life cycle linking river and sea

imageCaption: Temperate forest habitat used by wolves in Central Europe.
diet: Carnivore — deer, wild boar, beaver and smaller prey
distribution: Widespread across the Northern Hemisphere, including Europe, Asia and North America.
habitat: Forests, tundra, grassland and mountainous terrain; requires large connected landscapes.
physical: A large, highly adaptable canid with a broad muzzle, erect ears and a bushy tail.
behaviour: Lives in family packs with complex social hierarchies, cooperative hunting and scent communication.
reproduction: Breeding pairs produce a litter of four to six pups after a gestation of about 63 days.
description: A keystone predator whose return to European forests is changing prey behaviour and ecosystem dynamics. Białowieża is one of its important lowland strongholds.

imageCaption: Old-growth redwood forest habitat of the spotted owl.
diet: Carnivore — flying squirrels, woodrats and other small mammals
distribution: Western North America from British Columbia to southern Mexico, in three subspecies.
habitat: Mature and old-growth forest with complex structure, large trees and closed canopy.
physical: A medium-sized dark-brown owl with white spots, dark eyes and a rounded facial disc.
behaviour: Territorial and largely resident. Requires large home ranges and benefits from structurally complex forest.
reproduction: Pairs nest in tree cavities or platforms. Clutch size varies with prey availability, typically one to three eggs.
description: An old-growth forest specialist whose decline became a symbol of the conflict between logging and conservation in the Pacific Northwest.
keyTraits: Sensitive to forest fragmentation and barred owl competition
references: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service — spotted owl

imageCaption: Daintree rainforest understorey, habitat of the Ulysses butterfly.
diet: Nectar; larvae feed on selected rainforest plants
distribution: North-eastern Australia, New Guinea and nearby islands.
habitat: Tropical rainforest, forest edges and gardens.
physical: A large swallowtail butterfly with brilliant iridescent blue upper wings and dark margins.
behaviour: Males patrol forest edges and sunlit gaps; the bright blue flash is visible at a distance and can be used to track individuals.
reproduction: Females lay eggs on specific host plants. Larvae develop through several instars before pupating.
description: One of the most spectacular butterflies of the Wet Tropics. Its electric blue wings are produced by structural colour rather than pigment.
references: Atlas of Living Australia — Papilio ulysses

imageCaption: Congo Basin rainforest, habitat of the Goliath beetle.
diet: Adults feed on fruit and tree sap; larvae feed on decaying plant matter
size: Up to 11 cm, one of the world’s heaviest insects
distribution: Equatorial forests of West and Central Africa.
habitat: Lowland tropical rainforest with abundant decaying wood and fruiting trees.
physical: A massive scarab beetle with a black-and-white patterned body; males have a Y-shaped horn used in contests.
behaviour: Adults are attracted to fermenting fruit and sap. Larvae live in rich, decaying organic matter and take months to develop.
reproduction: Females lay eggs in decaying plant material; larvae pass through several stages before pupating in a soil cell.
description: Among the heaviest beetles on Earth, the Goliath beetle is a rainforest recycler whose larvae help break down decaying plant matter.
keyTraits: One of the world’s heaviest insects

imageCaption: Flooded igapó forest, the river dolphin’s seasonal habitat.
diet: Piscivore — fish, crustaceans and small aquatic animals
distribution: Amazon and Orinoco river systems of South America.
habitat: Main river channels, tributaries, lakes and flooded forest during the wet season.
physical: A freshwater dolphin with a long beak, flexible neck, pink-to-grey skin and small eyes. Adults often become pinker with age.
behaviour: Uses echolocation to navigate murky water and flooded forest. Often swims alone or in small groups and can move between rivers and floodplain lakes.
reproduction: Females give birth to a single calf after a long gestation; calves stay close to their mothers for an extended period.
description: Also called the pink river dolphin, the boto is the largest freshwater dolphin. It is threatened by dams, fishing gear, mercury pollution and river traffic.
keyTraits: Flexible neck for navigating flooded forest
Endangered by habitat fragmentation and pollution

imageCaption: Sundarban river channels, habitat of the saltwater crocodile.
diet: Carnivore — fish, reptiles, birds and mammals
distribution: Coastal waters, estuaries and rivers from eastern India through Southeast Asia to northern Australia.
habitat: Mangroves, estuaries, tidal rivers, swamps and coastal lagoons.
physical: The largest living reptile, with a broad snout, armoured skin, powerful tail and salt glands that allow survival in marine environments.
behaviour: Apex predator of estuarine systems. Adults defend territories and can travel long distances along coastlines. Usually ambush prey at the water’s edge.
reproduction: Females build nest mounds and guard the eggs. Hatchlings are vulnerable to predation and remain near nursery wetlands.
description: Saltwater crocodiles connect freshwater rivers, mangroves and the open sea. Their recovery after historical overhunting shows how large predators can return when protected.
